query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled trace addition of yttrium into the boride layer will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Y2O3-enhanced oxide scale that acts as an effective barrier against molten-aluminum attack, thereby improving the corrosion resistance of boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components as currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, with their standard alloy composition and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled amount of yttrium into the boride during its fabrication (e.g., via alloying or surface modification) so that yttrium is uniformly distributed in the coating.
generation.conditions: Test samples should be prepared with and without yttrium doping and then exposed to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (approximately 660 °C) for a duration representative of service conditions, under controlled thermal cycling if applicable.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a modified surface oxide layer that includes Y2O3 in addition to native oxides on the boride surface.
generation.mechanism: The yttrium addition is expected to facilitate the development of a dense, adherent oxide scale. Y2O3 is known to improve oxide scale stability and adhesion, which limits oxygen and aluminum interdiffusion. This results in a self-healing barrier that slows down the dissolution or degradation of the underlying boride when in contact with molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated boride-based components, the yttrium-doped components will exhibit a lower corrosion rate and fewer or less extensive signs of molten-aluminum induced degradation (e.g., lower mass loss and reduced oxide spallation).
generation.baseline: Boride-based components fabricated without yttrium doping and subjected to the same molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to hold as long as the yttrium content remains within an optimal trace level that does not alter the fundamental boride microstructure and when operating under typical hot-dip plating process temperatures (approximately 660 °C).
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal yttrium concentration and the long-term stability of the Y2O3-enhanced oxide scale under cyclic thermal stresses are not yet well established and require further experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of boride-based samples: one set in the standard composition (control) and one set doped with the trace level of yttrium. Subject both sets to molten-aluminum exposure at approximately 660 °C for an equivalent service duration. After exposure, perform a comparative analysis of mass loss, surface oxide morphology, and chemical composition.
measurements: Surface oxide layer characterization using SEM/EDS
Adhesion and spallation tests on the oxide scale
Microstructural analysis of the near-surface region
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in mass loss, improved oxide scale integrity (e.g., reduced spallation and more uniform coverage), and better overall resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. The oxide scale morphologies of the coatings are shown in Figure 10c,g and the EDS analysis is shown in Table 4. It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA. In conclusion, all coatings exhibited the same corrosion mechanism. The YHf-EHEA coating showed better resistance to the 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts hot corrosion than the EHEA coating at 900 °C.
